passage:
Thursday
Started watching one video about the exam paper leak last week. Fair enough, it WAS unfair, we all studied for nothing. Now my whole feed is angry people. Every single video. Scandals, cheats, 'they're laughing at you'. It feels like the whole country is on fire and nobody else sees it.
Posted my first proper rant on Monday. 23 likes. Normally I get like 4.
Today I posted a harsher one, called the officials 'parasites', and it got 140. People I don't even know commented 'finally someone says it'. My heart was racing all through maths.
Ankita said at lunch, 'You've changed. You're always on that stuff.' I said she's just scared of the truth. She went quiet.
I keep checking the count. I'm already thinking what to write next, something that'll hit harder.
— Francis

qa.q: How many likes did the harsher post get?
qa.a: It got 140 likes.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling while the likes came in?
qa.a: Francis felt a thrill and a rush of being noticed, with a racing heart, which pulled toward posting even harsher things.

qa.q: What could Francis try at this point to break the loop?
qa.a: Francis could notice that the feed is showing only angry content, take a break, unfollow or mute the rage accounts, and talk to Ankita or a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel after being told she's scared of the truth?
qa.a: Ankita may feel hurt and pushed away, when she was only worried about her friend.

grounding: It shows a teen clicking on angry content, the feed filling with more, and growing likes rewarding sharper, harsher posts.

passage:
It was the night before the chemistry exam, the fan was off because of a power cut, and Gurleen's phone was at nineteen per cent. She meant to check one thing. Instead she clicked an angry video about coaching centres cheating students, and the next one was angrier, and the next.
By eleven her whole feed was rage: people yelling, captions in red capitals. It began to feel as if the entire world was furious and lying.
She posted a short clip of her own: "They're all frauds and you're idiots if you trust them." In an hour it had four hundred likes, more than anything she had ever posted. Tejas from class cheered in the comments.
Her heart raced. She deleted a softer draft and wrote a harsher one. It got more.
At 1 a.m., battery at two per cent, chemistry book untouched, she was still refreshing, her jaw aching from clenching.

qa.q: How many likes did Gurleen's clip get in an hour?
qa.a: Four hundred likes.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she kept refreshing at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: She felt a racing thrill from the likes mixed with tense anger, her jaw aching, hooked on the rush.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Gurleen right now?
qa.a: Putting the phone away for the night, noticing that the feed changed because of her clicks, and talking the next day about what is really bothering her.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Gurleen's harsh post?
qa.a: Tejas may find it exciting to cheer on, without seeing how it is pulling Gurleen deeper into anger.

grounding: On an exam night a teen's clicks fill her feed with rage, and quick likes reward her for harsher and harsher posts.

passage:
Chandrika had only wanted to understand why local train fares went up. Two weeks later her feed was a wall of shouting: men pointing at cameras, headlines in capital letters, clips cut to make everyone look stupid or evil.
She had started commenting. Her mildest comments got nothing. Her nastiest got hundreds of replies and likes, and an account with ten thousand followers shared her line: "Anyone who defends this is a traitor." Chandrika read the notifications in the school washroom and felt her heart pound, half proud, half sick.
At dinner Vandana mentioned the fare rise and Chandrika snapped, "Everyone knows it's a scam, Mummy, open your eyes."
Vandana put down her spoon. "Since when do you talk to me like that?"
Chandrika didn't know. She only knew that the feed felt like the real world now, and home felt small and slow.

qa.q: What line of Chandrika's did the big account share?
qa.a: Anyone who defends this is a traitor.

qa.q: What did Chandrika feel reading the notifications in the washroom?
qa.a: She felt half proud and half sick, excited by the attention yet uneasy about how harsh she had become.

qa.q: What could help Chandrika notice what the feed is doing?
qa.a: Seeing that her clicks and nasty comments trained the feed, and talking calmly with Vandana about why the fare rise upset her.

qa.q: What is it like for Vandana when Chandrika snaps at dinner?
qa.a: Vandana is shocked and hurt by the new tone, unsure where her daughter's anger is coming from.

grounding: A teen's clicks turn her feed into a wall of outrage, and attention for her harshest comments makes the feed feel like the whole world.

passage:
"Look at my numbers," Harish said, pushing his phone at Vikas. "Eight thousand views. On one comment."
"What did you say?"
"That the college admissions thing is rigged and anyone who can't see it is a sheep."
"Harsh."
"Harsh gets views! Last week I wrote something normal, like, 'this seems unfair, let's ask for answers.' Nobody cared. Nine likes."
"So you just... turn it up?"
"The app keeps showing me more of this stuff anyway. My whole feed is people shouting now. It's like the whole country is angry."
"Mine isn't."
"Because you don't click on anything real."
"Maybe my feed's just different, not unreal. You look tired, bhai."
"I'm fine." Harish refreshed. "Ten thousand. See? People are listening."

qa.q: How many likes did Harish's normal comment get?
qa.a: Nine likes.

qa.q: What does Harish's constant refreshing suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels hooked and excited by the attention, while angry and tired underneath.

qa.q: What could Harish try to break this loop?
qa.a: Notice that harsher posts get rewarded, mute some rage accounts, and compare his feed with Vikas's to see it is not the whole world.

qa.q: How does Vikas see Harish's new habit?
qa.a: Vikas is uneasy and concerned, noticing that Harish looks tired and that his feed has become all shouting.

grounding: A teen finds that harsh comments earn far more attention than calm ones, and his feed of outrage starts to look like the whole world.

passage:
My name is Minakshi, and this happened in the summer before Class 11. I clicked one video about the fee hike at our coaching centre. It was angry and funny, and I watched it twice. By the next day my whole feed was fee hikes, then "useless teachers," then "this generation is being robbed." I remember thinking, wow, everyone is furious, not just me.
I posted a small comment and got forty likes. So the next one was sharper. I called a teacher a fraud; two hundred likes. My chest would buzz every time the number went up. Devika, my best friend, sent me a normal video of her cat, and I felt nothing. It seemed so small compared to my important anger. Looking back, I can see I had stopped scrolling for news. I was scrolling for that buzz.

qa.q: How many likes did Minakshi's first small comment get?
qa.a: Minakshi's first small comment got forty likes.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling each time the likes went up?
qa.a: Minakshi felt a thrilling buzz of excitement and importance, which made the anger feel rewarding.

qa.q: What turning point could Minakshi have used at that point in the summer?
qa.a: Minakshi could have noticed that the posts were getting harsher for likes, taken a break from the feed, and talked it over with Devika or a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when her cat video got no reply?
qa.a: Devika may have felt ignored and puzzled, sensing her best friend was drifting into something that left no room for ordinary things.

grounding: Shows a teenager clicking angry content until the feed feels like the whole world, with outrage rewarded by likes and posts getting harsher.
